as_told.place_text: University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill

plain: In the 1950s, the story goes, a wealthy North Carolina industrialist named Agnew Bahnson paid to set up a physics institute at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and put a young physicist named Bryce DeWitt in charge of it. The researcher Eric Weinstein tells it on two occasions without naming a source. The first time he is unsure of the man's name, calling him "bainson" with "some sort of tobacco or air conditioning fortune". The second time he says Bahnson worked with the physicist John Wheeler to find DeWitt, describes the place as an institute for anti-gravity, and points to an old newspaper clipping. Jesse Michels tells it twice in his own words. He names it the Institute of Field Physics, links it to a 1957 conference at Chapel Hill attended by the physicists Richard Feynman, Peter Bergmann, Freeman Dyson and John Wheeler, and says its work "often" concerned gravitational anomalies. The tellers bring it up because, if a private fortune was funding gravity research in those years, it would suggest serious early interest in ways to control gravity.
